---
title: "Design capacities of outlets and pumps"
---

The polder models set the unknown capacities (`max_flow_rate`) of Outlets and Pumps from the area they drain or supply, with the same design flow rates as the parametrization of the vrij afwaterend models.
The implementation lives in [`src/ribasim_nl/ribasim_nl/design_capacities.py`](https://github.com/Deltares/Ribasim-NL/tree/main/src/ribasim_nl/ribasim_nl/design_capacities.py), and the design flow rates in the defaults of [`ribasim_nl.parametrization.static_data_xlsx`](https://github.com/Deltares/Ribasim-NL/tree/main/src/ribasim_nl/ribasim_nl/parametrization/static_data_xlsx.py).

## Design flow rates

| Function | Node type | Design flow rate | Area |
|---|---|---|---|
| drain | Pump | 15 mm/day | its share of the drainage, see below |
| drain | Outlet | 50 mm/day | its share of the drainage, see below |
| supply | Pump or Outlet | 4 mm/day | Basins downstream, up to the drain nodes |
| flow_control | Pump or Outlet | the larger of drain and supply | both |

The function of each node comes from the `from_to_node_function_table`.
A supply node that supplies no Basin, such as one out of the model, supplies the area upstream instead.
The area of bergend Basins is left out, as it is the same as that of their doorgaand Basin.

## Splitting the drainage over the outflows

Basins joined by resistances or Junctions count as one water body.
Each water body drains its own area plus what the drains into it carry, and this drainage is split over the drains out of it:

- drains with a known capacity carry up to that capacity, and
- the other drains share the rest equally.

The drained area of a drain, times its design flow rate, is its design capacity.
Each unknown drain gets at least its share of the own area of its water body, so it keeps a capacity when the known drains can carry all.
Because the drainage is passed on from water body to water body, this repeats until the drained areas no longer change.
Where unknown drains form a loop that no unknown drain leaves, they would pass the drainage around forever, so in the water bodies of such a loop with known drains, these carry all.

In the example below, boezem B drains its own 2 km², the 6 km² of polders P1 and P2, and what comes back from polder C, over c, d and e.
Splitting gives c = d = e = 4.5 km² and f = 5.5 km², so c and d drain together the 9 km² of land to the boundary.
If every drain got the full area upstream instead, c and d would each get 9 km², and e and f around the loop too.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-split-drainage
%%| fig-cap: "Drained area in km² per drain when the drainage of each water body is split over its outflows."
flowchart LR
  P1["polder P1<br>4 km²"] -->|"a: 4"| B["boezem B<br>2 km²"]
  P2["polder P2<br>2 km²"] -->|"b: 2"| B
  B -->|"e: 4.5"| C["polder C<br>1 km²"]
  C -->|"f: 5.5"| B
  B -->|"c: 4.5"| S["boundary"]
  B -->|"d: 4.5"| S
```

## Limits from the neighbouring nodes

Finally, every unknown capacity is limited by the nodes around it.
A node carries no more than:

- the supply of the water body it flows into, plus the Pumps and Outlets out of it, and
- the drainage of the water body it comes from, plus the Pumps and Outlets into it.

Nodes straight between both water bodies are left out, so that nodes in opposite directions do not keep up each other's capacity.
The limits are applied repeatedly until no capacity changes, so that a small known pump also limits the outlets further upstream.
Flows from or to a boundary, or through another node without a capacity, such as a FlowBoundary, give no limit.

## Known capacities

Capacities with `meta_known_flow_rate` in the Pump and Outlet static tables are kept, as are those of nodes that drain or supply no Basin, such as an Outlet between two LevelBoundaries.
For the other nodes, the design capacity is the largest `max_flow_rate` of the node, and the other control states keep their ratio to it, so closed states stay closed.
The `flow_rate` of all nodes is set to their `max_flow_rate`, except in the control states that switch them off.

## Why not scale with simulations

Before, the capacities were scaled iteratively, by running design events and doubling or halving each capacity until the Basin levels stayed close to their target level.
This drove many capacities to the maximum of 50 m³/s, also where a larger capacity could not lower the level, such as behind a small known pump or in loops.
Such capacities on small Basins made the models stiff.
Capacities from the drained area scale with the flow that a node carries, and need no simulations.
